question: Which of the following is a continuous quantitative (numerical) variable?
options: The color of a student's eyes
The number of employees of an insurance company
The amount of milk in a 2-liter carton
The number of gallons of milk sold at the local grocery store yesterday
application: Use the continuous/discrete distinction before choosing summaries or probability models. A measured amount can take decimal values throughout an interval; a count changes in whole-number steps.
explanation: The amount of milk is measured and can be 1.982 L, 1.983 L, and so on, so it is continuous. Employee and gallon totals are counts; eye color is categorical.

visual.title: Measured values fill an interval
visual.caption: A continuous variable may take any value between two measurement marks.

question: Which of the following is most likely a population as opposed to a sample?
options: The first 5 students completing an assignment
Every third person to arrive at the bank
application: Define the target population before collecting data. A population contains every unit about which a conclusion is desired; a sample is only a subset selected from it.
explanation: Registered voters in the county describe the full target group. The other choices are subsets selected by voluntary response, convenience, or a systematic rule.

visual.title: Population contains every eligible unit
visual.caption: The sample sits inside the population and is used to learn about it.

question: A marketing research firm, in conducting a comparative taste test, provided three types of peanut butter to a sample of households randomly selected within the state. Which method of data collection is involved when people are asked to compare the three types?
application: Use an experiment when researchers deliberately assign or expose subjects to treatments and compare responses. Use a survey or observational study when no treatment is imposed.
explanation: The firm supplies three peanut-butter treatments and then measures preferences. Deliberately exposing households to alternatives makes this an experiment.

visual.title: Treatment creates the comparison
visual.caption: An imposed treatment is the feature that separates experimentation from passive observation.

question: True or False: Measurement error can become an ethical issue when a survey sponsor chooses leading questions that guide the responses in a direction.
application: Check wording, response scales, interviewer effects, and instrument calibration whenever a variable is measured. Systematic wording bias can distort results even with a large random sample.
explanation: A leading question systematically pushes answers toward the sponsor's preferred result. That creates measurement bias and is an ethical problem.

visual.title: Biased wording contaminates the measurement
visual.caption: Sampling quality cannot repair a question that measures responses unfairly.

question: When studying the simultaneous responses to two categorical questions, you should set up a ____.
application: Use a contingency table to study association between two categorical variables. Rows represent categories of one variable and columns represent categories of the other.
explanation: Cross-classifying both categorical responses produces joint cell counts, which is exactly the purpose of a contingency table.

visual.title: Two categories cross into cells
visual.caption: Each cell counts observations having one row category and one column category.

question:
An insurance agency recorded the number of claims X made by insured drivers in the last 3 years.

X | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5
f | 14 | 18 | 12 | 5 | 1

How many drivers are represented in the sample?
application: Use a frequency distribution to compress repeated observations. The total sample size is the sum of the frequency column, not the number of distinct X values.
explanation: Add the frequencies: 14 + 18 + 12 + 5 + 1 = 50 drivers.

visual.title: Frequencies rebuild the sample
visual.caption: Each frequency is a group of drivers; their sum is n.

question: A histogram gives the number of graduating seniors f who invited X guests: f(0)=17, f(1)=152, f(2)=85, f(3)=18, f(4)=3, f(5)=0. If all purchased tickets were used, how many guests attended the luncheon?
application: Use Σx·f when a frequency graph gives values and counts but the question asks for the total amount represented. Multiplying is essential because each person in a group contributes x units.

visual.title: Each bar contributes height × guest count
visual.caption: A weighted sum converts the histogram of seniors into a total number of guests.

question: True or False: In the displayed scatter plot of price/earnings ratio versus earnings per share for 20 U.S. companies, there appears to be a positive relationship.
application: Use a scatterplot to inspect direction, form, strength, and outliers for two quantitative variables before calculating a correlation or fitting a line.
explanation: The points generally move downward as earnings per share increases, indicating a negative rather than positive relationship.

visual.title: The point cloud slopes downward
visual.caption: A downward trend from left to right represents negative association.

question: True or False: The guidelines for developing visualizations recommend always starting the scale for a vertical axis at zero.
application: For bar and column charts, a zero baseline keeps lengths proportional to values and prevents small differences from appearing huge. If a nonzero baseline is necessary, mark the break conspicuously.
explanation: The course guideline treats a zero vertical baseline as the safe default for honest magnitude comparisons.

visual.title: The same values can look radically different
visual.caption: Truncating the vertical scale can visually amplify a small numerical difference.

question: The sorted ages of 25 senior citizens are 60, 61, 62, 63, 64, 65, 66, 68, 68, 69, 70, 73, 73, 74, 75, 76, 76, 81, 81, 82, 86, 87, 89, 90, 92. Determine the median age.
application: Use the median for an ordered dataset, especially when skewness or outliers make the mean unrepresentative. For odd n, select position (n+1)/2.
explanation: With n=25, the median is the 13th ordered observation, which is 73.

visual.title: Twelve observations lie on each side
visual.caption: The median is the central ordered value, not an average of all values.

question: Microwave prices at six stores are $111, $552, $158, $668, $355, and $312. Compute the range.
options: None of the other choices is correct
application: Use the range for a quick description of total spread. It is easy to compute but depends only on the minimum and maximum, so it is sensitive to extreme values.
explanation: Range = maximum − minimum = 668 − 111 = $557.

visual.title: Spread from the cheapest to the most expensive
visual.caption: Only the two endpoints determine the range.

question: The weights in ounces of three cookies are 0.71, 0.69, and 0.92. Compute the sample variance and round to one more decimal place than the original data.
options: None of the other choices is correct
application: Use sample variance to estimate population variability from sample data. Divide the sum of squared deviations by n−1 because the sample mean has already been estimated.
explanation: The mean is 0.7733. The squared deviations sum to about 0.03247; dividing by 2 gives s²≈0.0162, rounded to 0.016.

visual.title: Square deviations before averaging
visual.caption: Squaring makes deviations positive and gives larger departures more weight.

question: Determine the third quartile Q3 of the data: 5, 5, 5, 14, 7, 7, 8, 10, 11, 20, 24, 40, 45, 50, 51.
application: Use quartiles to divide ordered data into four parts and to build boxplots or the IQR. Always sort the observations before selecting quartile positions.
explanation: After sorting, the upper half is 20, 24, 40, 45, 50, 51 around its center; under the course position rule Q3 is the 12th ordered value, 40.

visual.title: Q3 marks the 75th-percentile boundary
visual.caption: About three quarters of the ordered observations are at or below Q3.

question: The population reuse-rate percentages for eight software analysts are 50, 62.5, 37.5, 75.0, 45.0, 47.5, 15.0, and 25.0. Find the population variance.
application: Use population variance when the data contain every unit in the defined population. Divide by N; use n−1 only when the observations are a sample used to estimate a larger population.
explanation: The population mean is 44.6875 and Σ(x−μ)²/N = 324.1211, so the variance rounds to 324.12.

visual.title: Population variance divides by N
visual.caption: The wording 'population of eight analysts' determines the denominator.

question: For variables X and Y, the sample covariance is 50. Which statement is true?
options: A positive covariance indicates that as X increases, Y tends to decrease.
A covariance of 50 means X and Y are perfectly positively correlated.
A positive covariance indicates that X and Y tend to increase or decrease together.
application: Use covariance to identify the direction of joint linear movement. Use correlation instead when a standardized, unit-free strength between −1 and 1 is needed.
explanation: A positive covariance means above-average X values tend to pair with above-average Y values and below-average values pair together. Its magnitude depends on units and does not imply perfect correlation.

visual.title: Same-sign deviations create positive products
visual.caption: Covariance averages products of deviations from the two means.

question: For a new car, P(repair)=0.05, P(U.S.-based manufacturer)=0.70, and P(repair and U.S.-based)=0.02. What is P(U.S.-based manufacturer or no warranty repair)?
options: None of the other choices is correct
application: Use the addition rule for an 'A or B' event: P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B). Complements often make 'not' events easier.
explanation: P(no repair)=0.95 and P(U.S. and no repair)=0.70−0.02=0.68. Therefore 0.70+0.95−0.68=0.97.

visual.title: Add both regions, subtract the overlap once
visual.caption: The overlap is contained in both marginal probabilities and must not be counted twice.

question:
For the contingency table below, what is P(D|C)?

      D | D′
C    12 | 18
C′   24 | 26
application: Use conditional probability when the question restricts attention to a known subgroup. The condition after the vertical bar becomes the new denominator.
explanation: Within row C there are 12+18=30 observations, and 12 also satisfy D. Thus P(D|C)=12/30=0.4.

visual.title: Condition on row C only
visual.caption: Once C is known, observations outside row C are excluded.

question: Among 200 restaurant customers, 75 were children and 125 adults; 120 preferred hamburgers and 80 chicken. Of the children, 55 preferred hamburgers. Given that a person prefers chicken, what is the probability the person is an adult?
options: None of the other choices is correct
application: Construct the missing cells of a two-way table before conditioning. This prevents mixing a joint count with the wrong marginal denominator.
explanation: Children choosing chicken =75−55=20, so adults choosing chicken =80−20=60. Conditional on 80 chicken customers, 60/80=75%.

visual.title: Complete the counts before dividing
visual.caption: The word 'given' changes the denominator to the chicken group.

question: A website password is a series of 4 different characters from English letters and digits. It must include exactly 2 letters, treating lower and upper case as the same. How many passwords satisfy the criteria?
application: Use combinations to choose which positions have a type of character, then permutations for distinct ordered selections within those positions.
explanation: Choose the 2 letter positions in C(4,2)=6 ways, then choose ordered distinct letters 26·25 and digits 10·9. Product: 6·26·25·10·9=351000.

visual.title: Choose slot types, then fill without replacement
visual.caption: Order matters for passwords, while the preliminary choice only locates character types.

question: A lab orders 100 rats in each of 52 weeks. The weekly price distribution is $10 with probability 0.35, $12.50 with probability 0.40, and $15 with probability 0.25. How much should it budget for next year's orders?
options: None of the other choices is correct
application: Use expected value for a long-run average cost under a stable probability distribution. Multiply each possible cost by its probability, sum, then scale by the number of repeated periods.

visual.title: Probability weights each possible weekly cost
visual.caption: Expected value is a planning average, not a claim that every week costs $12.25.

question: A manufacturer tests 16 television sets. Each set has a 5% defect probability. What is the probability that two or more sets are defective?
application: Use a binomial model for a fixed number of independent trials with the same success probability. For 'at least two', a complement is shorter than summing 2 through n.

visual.title: Remove zero and one from the whole distribution
visual.caption: Complement methods reduce many-tail calculations to a few easy terms.

question: Light-bulb failures follow a Poisson distribution. There were 4 failures over the last 20 weeks. Find the probability of no more than one failure next week.
options: None of the other choices is correct
application: Use Poisson probabilities for counts of events in a fixed interval when events occur independently at a stable average rate. Convert the observed rate to the same interval as the question.

visual.title: Convert the rate before applying Poisson
visual.caption: The Poisson parameter is the expected count in the target interval.

question: Investments X and Y have E(X)=$50 and E(Y)=$100. If the portfolio weight assigned to X is 0.6, compute the portfolio expected return.
options: None of the other choices is correct
application: Use a weighted average for the expected return of a portfolio. Variances and covariance are needed for portfolio risk, but not for the expected return.
explanation: The remaining weight on Y is 0.4. E(P)=0.6($50)+0.4($100)=$70.

visual.title: Weights must add to one
visual.caption: Linearity of expectation makes the portfolio mean a weighted average.

question: If Z is a standard normal random variable, find P(Z>−1.82). Given Φ(1.82)=0.9656.
options: None of the other choices is correct
application: Use symmetry of the standard normal distribution to convert a negative cutoff into a positive table entry: P(Z>−a)=P(Z<a)=Φ(a).
explanation: By symmetry, the area to the right of −1.82 equals the area to the left of +1.82, which is 0.9656.

visual.title: Mirror the cutoff across zero
visual.caption: Most of the normal curve lies to the right of a negative cutoff.

question: For a standard normal Z, P(Z>c)=0.1093. Find c. Given Φ(−1.23)=0.1093 and Φ(1.23)=0.8907.
options: None of the other choices is correct
application: Use a normal quantile when an area is known and the cutoff is unknown. Convert a right-tail area to a left cumulative area before reading the table.
explanation: P(Z>c)=0.1093 means Φ(c)=1−0.1093=0.8907. The supplied table associates 0.8907 with c=1.23.

visual.title: Right tail becomes a left cumulative area
visual.caption: The sign is positive because only about 11% lies above the cutoff.

question: Let X be uniform on [0,12]. What are the mean and variance of Y=3X?
application: For Y=aX+b, transform the mean with E(Y)=aE(X)+b and the variance with Var(Y)=a²Var(X). Adding a constant changes location but not spread.

visual.title: Scaling stretches location and spread differently
visual.caption: Variance uses the square of the scale factor.

question: Women's heights are normally distributed with mean 63.6 inches and standard deviation 2.5 inches. For a random sample of 90 women, find P(62.9<sample mean<64.0).
options: None of the other choices is correct
application: Use the sampling distribution of the mean for probabilities about an average from n observations. Its standard error is σ/√n, smaller than the individual standard deviation.

visual.title: Sample means cluster tightly around μ
visual.caption: A larger sample narrows the distribution of the sample mean.

question: Assume the true proportion of left-handed people is 10%. If 100 people are randomly chosen, what is the approximate probability that the sample proportion is no more than 9%?
application: Use the normal approximation for a sample proportion when np and n(1−p) are sufficiently large. Standardize with sqrt[p(1−p)/n].

visual.title: Locate 0.09 below the true proportion
visual.caption: The sampling distribution describes how sample proportions vary across repeated samples.

question: When constructing a 95% confidence interval for a population mean with known variance, which standard-normal critical value should be used? Let z0.05=1.645 and z0.025=1.96.
application: For a two-sided confidence interval, split α equally between two tails. A 95% interval has α=0.05 and α/2=0.025 in each tail.
explanation: The required critical value is z0.025=1.96.

visual.title: A 95% center leaves 2.5% in each tail
visual.caption: Using 1.645 would correspond to a one-sided 95% bound or a two-sided 90% interval.

question: In a random sample of 250 cellphone subscribers, 165 would upgrade at a reduced cost. Find the width of the 95% confidence interval for the true upgrade proportion.
options: None of the other choices is correct
application: Use p̂±z*√[p̂(1−p̂)/n] to estimate a population proportion. The interval width is twice the margin of error.

visual.title: Width spans two margins of error
visual.caption: Do not confuse interval width with the one-sided margin of error.

question: A bottled-water manager wants a 95% confidence estimate of the mean fill amount within ±0.005 gallon and assumes σ=0.01 gallon. What sample size is needed?
application: Use n=(z*σ/E)² when planning a mean estimate with known or conservatively estimated σ. Always round the result up so the requested precision is achieved.
explanation: n=(1.96·0.01/0.005)²=15.3664, which must be rounded up to 16.

visual.title: Precision determines required sample size
visual.caption: Rounding down would produce a margin larger than the requested tolerance.

question:
A researcher claims that 62% of voters favor gun control. Which symbolic hypotheses correctly express the claim?

(i) H0: π≥0.62, H1: π<0.62
(ii) H0: π=0.62, H1: π≠0.62
(iii) H0: π≠0.62, H1: π=0.62
(iv) H0: π<0.62, H1: π≥0.62
options: None of the other choices is correct
application: Place equality in H0. A claim of an exact value is tested against a two-sided alternative unless the wording explicitly says greater or less.
explanation: The exact claim π=0.62 belongs in H0 and the alternative is π≠0.62, which is statement (ii).

visual.title: Translate wording into symbols
visual.caption: The alternative hypothesis determines the rejection-tail direction.

question: Test the claim μ=300 with n=50, known population standard deviation, and significance level α=0.10. When should H0 be rejected?
options: Reject if the test statistic is greater than 2.575 or less than −2.575.
Reject if it is greater than 1.96 or less than −1.96.
Reject if it is greater than 1.645 or less than −1.645.
Reject if it is greater than 1.28 or less than −1.28.
None of the other choices is correct
application: For a two-sided z test, split α between two tails and reject when |z| exceeds zα/2.
explanation: The equality claim creates a two-sided test. With α/2=0.05, the critical values are ±1.645.

visual.title: Two rejection regions share α
visual.caption: The total probability of a Type I error remains 0.10.

question:
For H0: μ≤μ0 versus H1: μ>μ0, what is the critical value when testing a mean with unknown σ at significance level α?

(i) −tα,n−1
(ii) tα,n−1
(iii) tα/2,n−1
options: None of the other choices is correct
application: Use a t critical value when σ is unknown and estimated by the sample standard deviation. Tail direction comes from H1 and degrees of freedom are n−1.
explanation: H1 points right, so the rejection cutoff is the positive right-tail value tα,n−1, statement (ii).

visual.title: Unknown σ and a right-tailed alternative
visual.caption: Do not split α for a one-sided alternative.

question: Determine the test statistic for the population-proportion claim p>0.51, given n=50 and sample proportion p̂=0.61. Use α=0.01.
options: None of the other choices is correct
application: Use z=(p̂−p0)/√[p0(1−p0)/n] for a one-sample proportion test. The null value p0, not p̂, belongs in the standard error.
explanation: z=(0.61−0.51)/√(0.51·0.49/50)≈1.41. Alpha affects the critical cutoff, not the computed statistic.

visual.title: Standardize the observed proportion under H0
visual.caption: The sign is positive because the sample proportion exceeds the null value.

question: An unequal-variance two-sample t test compares mean business-start times for developed and emerging countries at α=0.05. Excel reports two-tail p-value=0.014681. What may be concluded?
options: There is no significant difference in the mean times.
There is a significant difference in the mean times.
Developed countries require significantly more time.
Developed countries require significantly less time.
application: Compare the p-value matching the alternative (one-tail or two-tail) with α. Reject H0 when p≤α; this establishes significance but direction should be stated only when the test and estimates support it.
explanation: The two-tail p-value 0.014681 is below 0.05, so reject equal means and conclude a significant difference.

visual.title: The p-value crosses the significance threshold
visual.caption: Use the two-tail p-value because the research question asks whether a difference exists.

question: The t test for the difference between the means of two independent populations assumes that the respective ____.
application: Use an independent-samples t procedure for unrelated groups. Check independence and approximate normality, especially with small samples; equal variances are required only for the pooled variant, not Welch's test.
explanation: Approximate population normality is the general small-sample distributional assumption. Sample sizes need not match, and Welch's t test does not require equal variances.

visual.title: Two separate groups feed one mean difference
visual.caption: Do not confuse independence of groups with equality of sample sizes.

question: The paired t-test is appropriate when ____.
options: Observations are taken in matched pairs or repeated measures
The variances of both populations are known
The differences between paired observations are approximately normally distributed
application: Use a paired t test for before/after measurements on the same units or deliberately matched units. Reduce each pair to a difference and analyze the mean difference.
explanation: Matched pairs or repeated measures create dependence within each pair, which is the design that calls for a paired t test. Approximate normality of differences is an assumption, not the defining design.

visual.title: Pair first, then subtract
visual.caption: The analysis is performed on differences, not on two independent columns.

question:
In testing for differences between the means of two related populations, which null hypothesis is correct?

(i) H0: μD≠0
(ii) H0: μD=0
(iii) H0: μD<0
application: For paired data define D consistently, such as after−before. 'No mean change' becomes μD=0; the research direction determines H1.
explanation: No difference between related population means is equivalent to a zero population mean difference, statement (ii).

visual.title: Two related means become one difference mean
visual.caption: Pairing converts a two-column problem into a one-sample hypothesis about D.

question: In samples of 150 women and 200 men, 62% of women and 24% of men answered yes to a workplace-harassment question. Find the test statistic for the claim that women's yes proportion is higher.
options: None of the other choices is correct
application: Use a pooled two-proportion z test when H0 states equal population proportions. Pool successes to estimate the common null proportion.
explanation: The pooled proportion is (0.62·150+0.24·200)/350≈0.4029. Standardizing 0.62−0.24 with the pooled SE gives z≈7.17.

visual.title: Observed gap relative to its null standard error
visual.caption: A very large positive z supports the directional claim.

question: When testing a difference between two population variances with sample sizes n1=15 and n2=20, where sample 1 has the larger variance, what numerator and denominator degrees of freedom are used?
options: None of the other choices is correct
application: Use an F ratio to compare two normal-population variances. Place the larger sample variance in the numerator for a right-tail setup; each variance contributes n−1 degrees of freedom.
explanation: The numerator df is 15−1=14 and the denominator df is 20−1=19.

visual.title: Each variance carries its own degrees of freedom
visual.caption: Degrees of freedom follow the variance's position in the F ratio.

question: The F test statistic in a one-way ANOVA is ____.
application: Use one-way ANOVA to compare three or more independent population means. The F ratio compares between-group variation (signal) with within-group variation (noise).
explanation: F=MSA/MSW: mean square among groups divided by mean square within groups.

visual.title: Signal divided by noise
nodes: Large F → evidence of different means
visual.caption: If group means are alike, both mean squares estimate the same variance and F stays near 1.

question: In a 2×2 factorial study of sign type and starting location, three subjects are assigned to each treatment combination. The ANOVA table has total df=11. What is the within-error degrees of freedom?
options: None of the other choices is correct
application: For a balanced a×b factorial design with n replicates per cell, error df=ab(n−1). It represents variation among observations receiving the same factor combination.
explanation: There are 2·2=4 cells and three subjects per cell, so error df=4(3−1)=8.

visual.title: Four cells, each with two residual degrees of freedom
visual.caption: Within-cell replication is what makes an independent error estimate possible.

question: In a regression line equation, what does the slope b1 represent?
options: The predicted value of Y when X=0
The estimated average change in Y per unit change in X
application: Use the slope to interpret how the fitted mean response changes with X. Always report its units and avoid causal language unless the study design supports causality.
explanation: b1 is the estimated change in predicted Y for a one-unit increase in X. The value at X=0 is the intercept b0.

visual.title: Slope is rise over one unit of run
visual.caption: Moving one unit right on the fitted line changes height by b1.

question: An Excel regression predicting GPA from ACT gives intercept 0.5681 and ACT coefficient 0.1021. Find the predicted GPA when ACT=20.
application: Use the fitted equation ŷ=b0+b1x for prediction within the observed X range. Read the coefficient table carefully: do not substitute Multiple R or a standard error for the intercept.

visual.title: Insert X into the fitted line
visual.caption: The prediction combines the baseline and the ACT-related change.

question: For X={4,5,8,9,10,13,15} and Y={9,7,16,22,20,28,38}, calculate the regression sum of squared errors SSE and choose the closest answer.
application: Use SSE=Σ(yi−ŷi)² to measure unexplained vertical variation around a fitted regression line. Smaller SSE means the fitted line tracks the observed responses more closely.
explanation: The fitted line is approximately ŷ=−4.1928+2.6461X. Squaring and summing its residuals gives SSE≈33.83, closest to 34.

visual.title: SSE adds squared vertical gaps
visual.caption: Squaring prevents positive and negative residuals from canceling.

question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four assumptions of linear regression?
application: Check linearity, independence, constant error variance, and approximate normality of errors before relying on regression inference. Residual plots and study design reveal different violations.
explanation: Regression assumes independence, not dependence, of errors. Dependence can understate uncertainty and invalidate standard tests.

visual.title: Regression diagnostic checklist
visual.caption: The incorrect choice reverses the independence requirement.

question:
You expect a positive population correlation between students' first two exam scores. Which hypotheses are appropriate?

(i) H0: ρ=1; H1: ρ<1
(ii) H0: ρ=0; H1: ρ>0
(iii) H0: ρ=0; H1: ρ≠0
(iv) H0: ρ=0; H1: ρ<0
application: Use a correlation hypothesis test to assess linear association in a population. The no-linear-association null is ρ=0; the research direction determines >, <, or ≠ in H1.
explanation: A positive-correlation claim requires H0:ρ=0 versus H1:ρ>0, statement (ii).

visual.title: A positive alternative looks for an upward trend
visual.caption: The null is not ρ=1; perfect correlation is not the default benchmark.

question:
A multiple regression of full-time job openings Y on worldwide revenues X1 and voluntary turnover X2 reports coefficients: intercept=91.73, X1=0.03, X2=44.19. Which fitted equation is correct?

(i) Ŷ=44.19+91.73X1+0.03X2
(ii) Ŷ=91.73+0.03X1+44.19X2
(iii) Ŷ=91.73+44.19X1+0.03X2
options: None of the other choices is correct
application: Build a multiple-regression equation by matching each coefficient row to its predictor. Interpret a slope as the change in predicted Y for one unit of that predictor while holding the others constant.
explanation: Place the intercept first and attach 0.03 to X1 and 44.19 to X2: Ŷ=91.73+0.03X1+44.19X2, statement (ii).

visual.title: Map coefficient rows to equation terms
visual.caption: The row labels, not the numerical size, determine which coefficient multiplies each predictor.

question: In a multiple regression model, which statement about adjusted R² is correct?
options: It has to be larger than the coefficient of multiple determination.
application: Use adjusted R² to compare models with different numbers of predictors because it penalizes unnecessary variables. Unlike ordinary R², it can fall when a weak predictor is added.
explanation: Adjusted R² can be negative when the fitted model performs worse after its degrees-of-freedom penalty than an intercept-only benchmark. It cannot exceed 1 and is no larger than ordinary R².

visual.title: Fit reward minus complexity penalty
visual.caption: Adding variables never decreases R², but can decrease adjusted R².
